ai.clinicalScope: Primary open‑angle glaucoma in adults presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Primary open‑angle glaucoma (POAG) is a chronic optic neuropathy caused by impaired aqueous outflow, leading to progressive visual field loss. In low‑resource settings, diagnosis relies on bedside assessment and simple tonometry, while treatment focuses on affordable IOP‑lowering eye drops and laser where available.

sections.p: POAG is a slowly progressive optic nerve disease characterised by elevated intra‑ocular pressure (IOP) with an open anterior chamber angle.
b: IOP > 21 mmHg on at least two readings
Normal‑looking angle on gonioscopy (if available)
Typical optic disc cupping (vertical cup‑disc ratio ≥0.6 or asymmetry ≥0.2)
Corresponding visual field defect

sections.p: Staging guides urgency of treatment and follow‑up frequency.
b: Early: IOP 22‑30 mmHg, mild cupping, no visual field loss
Moderate: IOP 31‑40 mmHg, cup‑disc ratio 0.7‑0.8, early peripheral field loss
Advanced: IOP >40 mmHg, cup‑disc ratio >0.8, central field loss, vision <20/200

sections.p: In primary disease the outflow resistance is idiopathic; secondary causes are common in the tropics and must be excluded.
b: Idiopathic trabecular meshwork dysfunction (most common)
Pigment dispersion (young men)
Pseudoexfoliation (elderly, especially with cataract)
Steroid‑induced (topical or systemic steroids)
Traumatic angle recession (post‑ocular injury)
Neovascular glaucoma (diabetic retinopathy, ocular TB, HIV‑related retinopathy)

sections.p: Patients often notice peripheral vision loss before any pain, making early detection difficult.
b: Gradual, painless loss of peripheral vision
Tunnel vision in advanced disease
Occasional halos around lights when IOP spikes
Rarely, acute ocular pain if angle closure supervenes

sections.p: Focus on tests that can be performed with limited equipment.

t.b: Is IOP elevated? – Confirms pressure component; if unavailable, use palpation to estimate high pressure.
Is there optic disc cupping? – Detects structural damage.
Are there characteristic field defects? – Confirms functional loss.
Is the angle open? – Differentiates POAG from angle‑closure.

b: Sudden IOP rise with severe eye pain → possible angle‑closure emergency
Rapid visual field loss over weeks
Neovascularisation of the iris (rubeosis iridis) → secondary glaucoma
Progressive optic disc pallor despite treatment

sections.p: Goal: lower IOP to a level that halts progression, using the most accessible options first.
b: First‑line topical beta‑blocker (timolol 0.5 %) – reduces aqueous production; avoid in asthma or severe COPD.
Adjunct prostaglandin analogue (latanoprost) – increases uveoscleral outflow; cheap generic versions are preferred.
If drops unavailable, consider oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (acetazolamide) for acute spikes; monitor renal function.
Laser trabeculoplasty (if laser available) – improves outflow, useful when adherence to drops is poor.
Surgical trabeculectomy reserved for refractory cases; requires postoperative follow‑up.

sections.p: Regular monitoring detects progression early and reinforces adherence.
b: IOP check every 3 months in early disease, every 1‑2 months if uncontrolled
Annual optic disc and visual field assessment
Educate patients on medication adherence and side‑effects
Screen first‑degree relatives over age 40
Avoid corticosteroid eye drops unless essential

sections.p: Conditions that mimic POAG either by similar visual loss or by raised IOP.
b: Angle‑closure glaucoma – presents with acute pain, mid‑dilated pupil, and a closed angle on gonioscopy.
Optic neuritis – painful eye movement, central scotoma, normal IOP.
Retinal detachment – sudden curtain‑like visual loss, normal IOP, peripheral retinal breaks.

sections.p: Be aware of false‑negative or misleading findings.
b: Normal IOP does not rule out normal‑tension glaucoma, especially in thin‑skinned African patients.
Cupping may be congenital; compare with fellow eye and look for progressive change.
Confrontation visual fields can miss early defects; rely on formal testing when possible.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe eye pain with halos and blurred vision
Rapid loss of vision over days
New onset of double vision or eye redness with pain

faq.q: Why is glaucoma called the 'silent thief of sight'?
faq.a: Because visual field loss occurs gradually and painlessly until central vision is affected.

faq.q: Can normal‑tension glaucoma occur in African patients?
faq.a: Yes; IOP may be within normal range, so optic disc assessment and fields are essential.

faq.q: Are beta‑blocker eye drops safe in patients with asthma?
faq.a: Topical timolol can be absorbed systemically; avoid or use prostaglandin analogue instead in severe asthma.

exam: A 55‑year‑old farmer presents with peripheral vision loss but no pain – what is your next diagnostic step? — Perform applanation tonometry to assess IOP and examine the optic disc.
How does primary open‑angle glaucoma differ from angle‑closure glaucoma on gonioscopy? — POAG shows an open angle; angle‑closure shows peripheral anterior synechiae and a closed angle.
A patient on timolol reports wheezing – what should you do? — Switch to a prostaglandin analogue because beta‑blockers can exacerbate bronchospasm.
Explain why laser trabeculoplasty is useful in low‑resource settings. — It reduces dependence on daily drops and can be performed with a single device for many patients.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent referral to an ophthalmic surgeon? — Sudden severe eye pain with a cloudy cornea suggesting acute angle‑closure.
How would you screen a sibling of a patient with POAG? — Measure IOP, perform optic disc examination, and arrange visual field testing if IOP is elevated.
Why might a normal IOP not exclude glaucoma in this population? — African patients can develop normal‑tension glaucoma; structural optic nerve changes are more reliable.
What is the rationale for avoiding chronic steroid eye drops in glaucoma patients? — Steroids increase trabecular meshwork resistance, raising IOP.
